hook: A dietitian surveys 400 randomly chosen students and finds that 62% regularly skip breakfast. She could report "62%" and stop, but another sample would give 59% or 65%. A confidence interval reports a range instead, built by a method that captures the true campus proportion a known share of the time.

prereq.q: Under the standard normal curve, what value has an area of 0.975 below it?
prereq.why: $P(Z \le 1.96) = 0.975$, so 95% of the area lies between $-1.96$ and $1.96$.

figure.caption: In 95% of samples, the sample proportion lands within 1.96 standard deviations of p, so the interval built around it reaches across p.

chain.effect: in 95% of random samples, $\hat{p}$ lands within 1.96 standard deviations of $p$
in 95% of samples, $p$ is within 1.96 standard deviations of $\hat{p}$

chain.cause: We do not know $p$, so the standard deviation cannot be computed
chain.effect: we use the standard error $\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}$ in its place

chain.cause: Go $z^*$ standard errors out on each side of $\hat{p}$
chain.effect: $\hat{p} \pm z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}$ captures $p$ for the stated share of samples

ideas: Interval = statistic ± (critical value)(standard error). For one proportion: $\hat{p} \pm z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}$.
Conditions in words: random sample; $n$ at most 10% of the population; at least 10 successes and 10 failures in the sample.
Margin of error $= z^* \cdot \text{SE}$. It shrinks with a larger $n$ (4 times $n$ halves it) and grows with the confidence level.
Name the procedure in full: one-sample z interval for a proportion.

misconception.wrong: For a 90% interval, find the $z$ with 0.90 of the area below it, so $z^* = 1.28$.
misconception.right: A 90% interval keeps 90% in the middle and leaves 5% in each tail, so $z^*$ has 0.95 below it: $z^* = 1.645$.

summary: A confidence interval for $p$ is $\hat{p} \pm z^*\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})/n}$: the point estimate plus or minus a margin of error. Check random, 10% and large counts (sample successes and failures at least 10) in words first. Larger samples shrink the margin of error; higher confidence levels stretch it.
